items.stem: What is the shape of an s orbital?
items.answer: spherical
items.markingKey: s orbitals are spherical; p orbitals are dumbbell-shaped along x, y and z axes.

items.stem: Explain why the 4s subshell fills before the 3d subshell.
items.answer: The 4s subshell is lower in energy than 3d (in atoms from K to Ca), so electrons occupy it first.
items.markingKey: 4s lower energy [1]; electrons fill lowest energy first [1]

items.stem: Describe the difference between a 1s and a 2s orbital.
items.answer: Both are spherical, but the 2s orbital is larger (further from the nucleus) and higher in energy.
items.markingKey: both spherical [1]; 2s larger/higher energy [1]

items.stem: What is the maximum number of orbitals in the shell with principal quantum number n = 2?
items.markingKey: orbitals: n² = 4.

items.stem: For an atom of carbon (proton number 6), state (i) the total number of electrons in p orbitals and (ii) the number of p orbitals that contain at least one electron.
items.markingKey: configuration 1s²2s²2p² [1]; (i) 2 [1]; (ii) count of occupied p orbitals [1]

items.stem: A teacher in Cape Town asks students to describe the orbitals occupied in an atom of calcium, Z = 20. (a) Write the full electronic configuration. (b) Explain why the 4s subshell is filled before 3d. (c) State the maximum number of electrons that the third shell can hold and how they are distributed among subshells.
items.answer: (a) 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶4s² (b) 4s is lower in energy than 3d. (c) 18: 3s 2, 3p 6, 3d 10.
items.markingKey: (a) 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶4s² [1] (b) 4s is lower in energy than 3d. [1] (c) 18: 3s 2, 3p 6, 3d 10. [2]

items.stem: How many orbitals are there in a p subshell?
items.markingKey: p subshell: px, py, pz — 3 orbitals, up to 6 electrons.

items.stem: Describe the shape and orientation of the 2p orbitals.
items.answer: Three dumbbell-shaped orbitals (2px, 2py, 2pz) arranged at right angles along the x, y and z axes, each with two lobes on either side of the nucleus.
items.markingKey: dumbbell [1]; three at 90° to each other [1]

items.stem: Explain the term subshell.
items.answer: A group of orbitals of equal energy within a shell, labelled s, p, d or f (1, 3, 5 or 7 orbitals).
items.markingKey: orbitals of same energy within a shell [1]; s/p/d with orbital numbers [1]

items.stem: "Electrons in an orbital move in a fixed circular path around the nucleus." Comment on this statement made by a student, correcting any error.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. An orbital is a region of space where there is a high probability of finding the electron(s); not a fixed orbit.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: What is the maximum number of orbitals in the shell with principal quantum number n = 1?
items.markingKey: orbitals: n² = 1.

items.stem: Ethan is studying the electron arrangement of nitrogen (proton number 7). (a) State the number of unpaired electrons, explaining how electrons occupy orbitals of equal energy. (b) Explain why the 4s subshell is filled before 3d.
items.answer: (a) 3; electrons occupy orbitals of equal energy singly (with parallel spins) before pairing, because this minimises repulsion. (b) 4s is lower in energy than 3d.
items.markingKey: (a) 3; electrons occupy orbitals of equal energy singly (with parallel spins) before pairing, because this minimises repulsion. [2] (b) 4s is lower in energy than 3d. [1]

items.stem: A teacher in Riyadh asks students to describe the orbitals occupied in an atom of chlorine, Z = 17. (a) Write the full electronic configuration. (b) State the number of occupied orbitals in the atom. (c) State the number of unpaired electrons, explaining how electrons occupy orbitals of equal energy.
items.answer: (a) 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁵ (b) 9 (c) 1; electrons occupy orbitals of equal energy singly (with parallel spins) before pairing, because this minimises repulsion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁵ [1] (b) 9 [1] (c) 1; electrons occupy orbitals of equal energy singly (with parallel spins) before pairing, because this minimises repulsion. [2]

items.stem: A teacher in Colombo asks students to describe the orbitals occupied in an atom of oxygen, Z = 8. (a) Write the full electronic configuration. (b) State the number of occupied orbitals in the atom. (c) State the number of unpaired electrons, explaining how electrons occupy orbitals of equal energy. (d) Explain why the 4s subshell is filled before 3d.
items.answer: (a) 1s²2s²2p⁴ (b) 5 (c) 2; electrons occupy orbitals of equal energy singly (with parallel spins) before pairing, because this minimises repulsion. (d) 4s is lower in energy than 3d.
items.markingKey: (a) 1s²2s²2p⁴ [1] (b) 5 [1] (c) 2; electrons occupy orbitals of equal energy singly (with parallel spins) before pairing, because this minimises repulsion. [2] (d) 4s is lower in energy than 3d. [1]

items.stem: What is the electronic configuration of chromium, Cr (Z = 24)?
items.answer: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁵4s¹
items.markingKey: Cr is an exception: a half-filled 3d⁵ subshell with 4s¹ is more stable.

items.stem: Explain why a chlorine atom is a free radical but a chloride ion is not.
items.answer: Cl (3p⁵) has an unpaired electron; Cl⁻ (3p⁶) has all electrons paired.
items.markingKey: Cl has unpaired electron [1]; Cl⁻ all paired [1]

items.stem: Explain, using box notation, why nitrogen has three unpaired electrons.
items.answer: The three 2p electrons occupy the three 2p orbitals singly with parallel spins (Hund’s rule) because this minimises repulsion.
items.markingKey: box diagram 2p↑ ↑ ↑ [1]; singly occupied to minimise repulsion [1]

items.stem: Write the full electronic configuration of an atom of krypton (Z = 36) and state the number of unpaired electrons.
items.answer: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d¹⁰4s²4p⁶; 0 unpaired
items.markingKey: configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d¹⁰4s²4p⁶ [1]; 0 unpaired (singly-filled orbitals before pairing) [1]

items.stem: Write the electronic configuration of an atom of krypton (Z = 36). Use box notation for the outer subshells to deduce the number of unpaired electrons and state whether it is a free radical.
items.answer: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d¹⁰4s²4p⁶; 0 unpaired electron(s); it is not a free radical
items.markingKey: configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d¹⁰4s²4p⁶ [1]; 0 unpaired (singly-filled orbitals before pairing) [1]; not a radical: all paired [1]

items.stem: Sipho is investigating compounds of chromium, Z = 24, which contain Cr³⁺ ions. (a) Write the full electronic configuration of a chromium atom. items.answer: (a) 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁵4s¹ (b) 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d³ (c) 3 unpaired electrons
items.markingKey: (a) 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁵4s¹ [1] (b) 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d³ [1] (c) 3 unpaired electrons [2]

items.stem: Which electrons are removed first when an iron atom forms the Fe²⁺ ion?
items.answer: the 4s electrons
items.markingKey: Transition-metal ions lose 4s electrons before 3d: Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶.

items.stem: Explain why copper has the configuration [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ rather than [Ar]3d⁹4s².
items.answer: A completely filled 3d subshell gives a more stable (lower energy) arrangement.
items.markingKey: full 3d more stable [1]; one 4s electron moves into 3d [1]

items.stem: Explain why the methyl radical, •CH₃, is very reactive.
items.answer: Carbon has an unpaired electron; the radical readily forms a bond by pairing that electron (e.g. with Cl•).
items.markingKey: unpaired electron [1]; pairs by forming bond [1]

items.stem: "The oxygen atom has no unpaired electrons because 2p⁴ is an even number." Comment on this statement made by a student, correcting any error.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. In 2p⁴ one orbital is paired and two are singly occupied, so O has two unpaired electrons.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Write the full electronic configuration of an atom of phosphorus (Z = 15) and state the number of unpaired electrons.
items.answer: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p³; 3 unpaired
items.markingKey: configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p³ [1]; 3 unpaired (singly-filled orbitals before pairing) [1]

items.stem: Arjun is investigating compounds of cobalt, Z = 27, which contain Co²⁺ ions. (a) Write the electronic configuration of the Co²⁺ ion. (b) Draw the box notation for the 3d and 4s subshells of Co²⁺ and state the number of unpaired electrons.
items.answer: (a) 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁷ (b) 3 unpaired electrons
items.markingKey: (a) 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁷ [1] (b) 3 unpaired electrons [2]

items.answer: (a) 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁶4s² (b) 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁶ (c) 4 unpaired electrons

items.answer: (a) 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁷ (b) 3 unpaired electrons (c) A species with an unpaired electron; yes, it has unpaired electrons (though as a stable ion it is not usually described as a reactive radical)

items.stem: Which equation represents the first ionisation energy of sodium?
items.answer: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻
items.markingKey: First IE: 1 mol of gaseous atoms → 1 mol of gaseous 1+ ions.

items.stem: Explain why there is a very large increase between the first and second ionisation energies of potassium.
items.answer: The second electron is removed from a shell closer to the nucleus (3p), with much less shielding, so it is held far more strongly.
items.markingKey: second electron from inner shell [1]; closer/less shielded so more attraction [1]

items.stem: Explain how a graph of successive ionisation energies provides evidence for electron shells.
items.answer: Large jumps occur when electrons start to be removed from a new shell closer to the nucleus; the number of electrons between jumps shows the number in each shell.
items.markingKey: big jumps between shells [1]; number of electrons in each shell [1]

items.stem: The successive ionisation energies of element X, in kJ mol⁻¹, are 503, 965, 3600. Deduce the group of X in the Periodic Table, explaining your reasoning.
items.answer: Group 2
items.markingKey: largest jump between second and third IE [1]; so 2 electron(s) in outer shell, Group 2 [1]

items.stem: The successive ionisation energies of element X, in kJ mol⁻¹, are 1402, 2856, 4578, 7475, 9445, 53,267. Deduce the group of X in the Periodic Table, explaining your reasoning.
items.answer: Group 15
items.markingKey: largest jump between fifth and sixth IE [1]; so 5 electron(s) in outer shell, Group 15 [1]

items.stem: Element X is in Period 2. Its successive ionisation energies (kJ mol⁻¹) are 1314, 3388, 5301, 7469, 10,990, 13,327, 71,330. Identify X, write an equation for its seventh ionisation energy and explain why this value is so much larger than the sixth.
items.answer: oxygen; O⁶⁺(g) → O⁷⁺(g) + e⁻; the seventh electron is removed from an inner shell, closer to the nucleus and less shielded.
items.markingKey: jump after 6 electrons: Group 16, so oxygen [1]; equation with state symbols [1]; inner shell/closer [1]; less shielding/greater attraction [1]

items.stem: Which factor does NOT affect the first ionisation energy of an atom?
options: the distance of the outer electron from the nucleus
the number of neutrons in the nucleus
items.answer: the number of neutrons in the nucleus
items.markingKey: IE depends on nuclear charge, distance of outer electron, shielding and spin-pair repulsion.

items.stem: Why do successive ionisation energies of an element always increase?
options: the nuclear charge increases after each ionisation
each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion
electrons are removed from inner shells first
items.answer: each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion
items.markingKey: Fewer electrons remain for the same nuclear charge, so attraction for each is greater.

items.stem: State and explain three factors that affect the size of an ionisation energy.
items.answer: Nuclear charge (more protons, higher IE); distance of the electron from the nucleus (further, lower IE); shielding by inner electrons (more shielding, lower IE). Spin-pair repulsion lowers IE.
items.markingKey: one mark per factor with direction [3]

items.stem: Explain why the second ionisation energy of an element is always larger than its first.
items.answer: The second electron is removed from a positive ion; the same nuclear charge attracts fewer electrons, so there is less repulsion and greater attraction.
items.markingKey: removed from positive ion [1]; greater attraction/less repulsion [1]

items.stem: In a test answer, Arjun states: "The first ionisation energy is the energy released when an electron is added to an atom." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. It is the energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in 1 mol of gaseous atoms (endothermic).
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Element X has the successive ionisation energies (kJ mol⁻¹) 550, 1064, 4138, 5500. How many electrons are in the outer shell of X?

items.stem: What is the general trend in first ionisation energy across Period 3 from Na to Ar?
items.answer: it increases

items.stem: Explain the general increase in first ionisation energy across Period 3.
items.answer: Nuclear charge increases, electrons are added to the same shell so shielding is similar; atomic radius decreases so the outer electron is held more strongly.
items.markingKey: nuclear charge increases [1]; same shell/similar shielding [1]

items.stem: Explain why the first ionisation energy of aluminium is lower than that of magnesium.
items.answer: Al’s outer electron is in a 3p orbital, higher in energy than 3s and partly shielded by the 3s electrons, so it is easier to remove.
items.markingKey: 3p vs 3s [1]; higher energy/extra shielding [1]

items.stem: Four consecutive elements W, X, Y and Z in Period 2 have first ionisation energies of W 1402, X 1314, Y 1681, Z 2081 kJ mol⁻¹. Identify the four elements and explain why the first ionisation energy of X is lower than that of W.
items.answer: W = nitrogen, X = oxygen, Y = fluorine, Z = neon. In O the 2p⁴ electron removed is paired in an orbital; spin-pair repulsion makes it easier to remove, so O has the lower first IE.
items.markingKey: dip identifies Group 16 [1]; all four identified [1]; explanation (spin-pair repulsion) [1]

items.stem: Four consecutive elements W, X, Y and Z in Period 3 have first ionisation energies of W 787, X 1012, Y 1000, Z 1251 kJ mol⁻¹. Identify the four elements and explain why the first ionisation energy of Y is lower than that of X.
items.answer: W = silicon, X = phosphorus, Y = sulfur, Z = chlorine. In S the 3p⁴ electron removed is paired; spin-pair repulsion makes it easier to remove, so S has the lower first IE.
items.markingKey: dip identifies Group 16 [1]; all four identified [1]; explanation (spin-pair repulsion) [1]

items.stem: Explain why the first ionisation energy of sulfur is lower than that of phosphorus.
items.answer: In S the electron is removed from a 3p orbital containing a pair of electrons; spin-pair repulsion makes it easier to remove.
items.markingKey: paired electron in 3p [1]; repulsion [1]

items.stem: Diego is investigating compounds of copper, Z = 29, which contain Cu⁺ ions. (a) Write the electronic configuration of the Cu⁺ ion. (b) Explain which electrons are lost when the ion forms. (c) Draw the box notation for the 3d and 4s subshells of Cu⁺ and state the number of unpaired electrons. (d) Name another species with the same electronic configuration as Ar.
items.answer: (a) 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d¹⁰ (b) The 4s electrons are lost first (then 3d), because once 3d is occupied the 4s electrons are higher in energy / further from the nucleus. (c) 0 unpaired electrons (d) e.g. K⁺, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻, S²⁻

items.stem: Which equation represents the fourth ionisation energy of chlorine?
items.answer: Cl³⁺(g) → Cl⁴⁺(g) + e⁻
items.markingKey: Fourth IE: remove one electron from each gaseous ion: Cl³⁺(g) → Cl⁴⁺(g) + e⁻.

items.stem: In a test answer, Nadia states: "The first ionisation energy is the energy released when an electron is added to an atom." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. It is the energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in 1 mol of gaseous atoms (endothermic).
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Sofia is plotting successive ionisation energies from a data book. (a) Explain why the second ionisation energy of an element is always larger than its first. (b) Explain how a graph of successive ionisation energies provides evidence for electron shells.
items.answer: (a) The second electron is removed from a positive ion; the same nuclear charge attracts fewer electrons, so there is less repulsion and greater attraction. (b) Large jumps occur when electrons start to be removed from a new shell closer to the nucleus; the number of electrons between jumps shows the number in each shell.
items.markingKey: (a) removed from positive ion; greater attraction/less repulsion [2] (b) big jumps between shells; number of electrons in each shell [2]

items.stem: The successive ionisation energies of element X, in kJ mol⁻¹, are 520, 7298, 11,815. Deduce the group of X in the Periodic Table, explaining your reasoning.
items.answer: Group 1

(a) Explain the large increase between the second and third ionisation energies. (b) Q is in Period 3. Identify Q and write the electronic configuration of its atom.
items.answer: (a) The electron is removed from a new shell closer to the nucleus with less shielding. (b) magnesium: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²

items.stem: Explain why the first ionisation energy decreases down Group 2 even though nuclear charge increases.
items.answer: The outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus and is more shielded by inner shells; these effects outweigh the extra nuclear charge.
items.markingKey: further/more shells [1]; more shielding outweighs nuclear charge [1]

items.stem: A student in Karachi claims that the first ionisation energy of oxygen is higher than nitrogen because oxygen has more protons. Is the student correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. O is lower than N: the electron removed from O is paired in a 2p orbital and spin-pair repulsion makes it easier to remove.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Four consecutive elements W, X, Y and Z in Period 3 have first ionisation energies of W 578, X 787, Y 1012, Z 1000 kJ mol⁻¹. Identify the four elements and explain why the first ionisation energy of Z is lower than that of Y.
items.answer: W = aluminium, X = silicon, Y = phosphorus, Z = sulfur. In S the 3p⁴ electron removed is paired; spin-pair repulsion makes it easier to remove, so S has the lower first IE.
items.markingKey: dip identifies Group 16 [1]; all four identified [1]; explanation (spin-pair repulsion) [1]

items.stem: The table shows first ionisation energies (kJ mol⁻¹) for Period 2, studied by a class in Toronto: Li 520, Be 900, B 801, C 1086, N 1402, O 1314, F 1681, Ne 2081. (a) Describe and explain the general trend across the period. (b) Explain why boron has a lower first IE than beryllium.
items.answer: (a) Increases: nuclear charge increases, same shell, similar shielding. (b) Outer electron of B in a p subshell: higher energy, shielded by s electrons.

items.stem: Which subshell is filled immediately after 4s?
items.answer: 3d

items.stem: A class in Singapore is studying the arrangement of electrons in shells and subshells. Explain the term subshell.
items.answer: A group of orbitals of equal energy within a shell, labelled s, p, d or f (1, 3, 5 or 7 orbitals).
items.markingKey: orbitals of same energy within a shell; s/p/d with orbital numbers [2]

items.stem: What is the maximum number of electrons in the shell with principal quantum number n = 3?
items.markingKey: electrons: 2n² = 18.

items.stem: A teacher in Manila asks students to describe the orbitals occupied in an atom of calcium, Z = 20. (a) Write the full electronic configuration. (b) Sketch and describe the shape of an s orbital and of a p orbital.
items.answer: (a) 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶4s² (b) s: sphere centred on the nucleus; p: dumbbell (two lobes) along an axis.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) State and explain three factors that affect the size of an ionisation energy. (b) Explain why the second ionisation energy of an element is always larger than its first.
items.answer: (a) Nuclear charge (more protons, higher IE); distance of the electron from the nucleus (further, lower IE); shielding by inner electrons (more shielding, lower IE). Spin-pair repulsion lowers IE. (b) The second electron is removed from a positive ion; the same nuclear charge attracts fewer electrons, so there is less repulsion and greater attraction.
items.markingKey: (a) one mark per factor with direction [3] (b) removed from positive ion [1]; greater attraction/less repulsion [1]
